messages.content: Write a customer case study about a company that adopted a continuous delivery platform and now deploys more often. Around 250 words.

output:
Since you didn't name a customer, I wrote it as an illustrative case study — the company, quotes, and numbers are invented, and the platform name is a `[Platform]` placeholder. Swap in real data before it goes anywhere public. It passes this repo's `slopwatch` and `codewatch` gates, 237 words.

---

**Rivermark Logistics: from Thursday-night releases to 40 deploys a week**

Rivermark ships freight-tracking software to about 200 regional carriers. Two years ago, a release meant a Thursday evening war room: eleven people on a call, a 90-minute manual checklist, and a rollback plan nobody had tested since March.

"We deployed every three weeks because that was as often as we could stomach it," says Dana Okonjo, Rivermark's VP of Engineering.

The team moved to [Platform] in January 2024. The first six weeks were unglamorous, mostly untangling a build script that had grown to 1,400 lines and standing up test environments close enough to production to trust. The manual checklist went from 42 items to four, then to none.

Where they landed, measured last quarter: 41 deploys per week, up from roughly one every three weeks. Merge-to-production time fell from 19 days to 2 hours 20 minutes. Change failure rate dropped from 22% to 6%, which nobody expected; the team had assumed shipping more often would break more things. Smaller diffs turned out to be easier to review and much easier to revert.

The Thursday war room is gone. Rollbacks happen about twice a month, take under four minutes, and no longer need a phone tree.

Okonjo is blunt about the cost: "We spent close to a quarter of an engineer-year on pipeline work that shipped zero features. I'd do it again. I wouldn't pretend it was free."
